doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

title: Deciding on a career; early gigs and school
summary: She decided on a career around 1968 but was working at twelve; as a teen she played six nights a week at a Latin club and found school of little value.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Very interesting. Was there a point where you said to yourself I’m going to make a career out of this?

Yes but it was much, much later than you would think. I’d been doing it for a very long time. I would say, let’s see, it was one year before people began to know who I was. 1968, I thought, you know I think I want to really do this. I didn’t really define what it was or who I wanted to do it with but that I think was already defined in what I heard and what I felt and the people who played in that kind of an essence. A strong, a kind of a really strong feeling.
Did you do non-musical work before, to make a living, before you kind of jumped into the music thing?
No I mean I was always a musician.
Yeah, yeah. I started when I was eleven, so I was working by the time I was twelve.
Can you remember what you made on your first paying gig?

No. I don’t. But well there was one that I do remember, because I remember being able to go out and buy a coat, a cashmere coat. This was so long ago, of what would be the — what it would be now I can’t imagine. I guess if you would times it by twenty, it would

be maybe about two thousand dollars a week now, what it was then. But that was when I was a teenager. I was still in high school and I was working six nights a week in this club. It was like a Latin club, it was called the Million Dollar Theater and we played Latin music. So that was fun. Six nights a week and then I had to try to get to school the next day.
Did your friends think that was pretty outrageous?
Only a few people knew. I didn’t tell everybody. Because that was another world that was busy, and then there was the school world.
Yeah. Were you anxious to get out of public school?

I didn’t really think school had much value for me after the age of ten or eleven. I had a few teachers that I did like, and I liked the way they taught, and that’s what intrigued — I wouldn’t care what the subject was, there were a few teachers, but not too many. Most of it I thought was kind of a waste of time.
